implementation_notes: Structured concurrency is the language-level realization: the documentation describes TaskGroup as a group that contains dynamically created child tasks, so a loop over the runtime recipient set calls addTask { await recipient.deliver(copy) } and withTaskGroup does not return until every child task has completed. Cancellation is structural - cancelAll() marks the children and each checks Task.isCancelled - and async let is only the fixed-arity form, which is why the dynamic case is a group. No router component is needed; what remains application code is the recipient resolution and the decision to continue or abort on failure.
pitfalls: A task group always awaits its children: returning early from the body does not skip the remaining deliveries - call group.cancelAll() and have each child check Task.isCancelled.
Child tasks inherit the parent's actor isolation and priority, so calling deliver on a main-actor type serialises the whole fan-out on the main thread.
Capturing a non-Sendable recipient or a mutable message inside addTask is a compile error under strict concurrency; pass value copies or Sendable handles.
